title: Education Gadfly Weekly: Hannah-Jones, AI Bans, and Ohio Advanced Math
author: Fordham Institute
source: fordhaminstitute.org (Education Gadfly Weekly, Vol. 26, No. 39), October 1, 2026
summary: This issue of the Thomas B. Fordham Institute's Education Gadfly Weekly (Volume 26, Number 39) curates three commentary pieces and two study reviews. Robert Pondiscio uses Nikole Hannah-Jones's account of her daughter's school to argue that good schools need both responsibility and competence. Emily Freitag argues against banning AI in schools, urging observation of real-world effects before regulation. Aaron Churchill explains Ohio's new automatic-enrollment advanced-math policy. The reviews cover research on whether dual-enrollment students benefit even when they fail college courses and a study of the spread of no-zero grading policies across 295 Washington State districts. The issue also announces the annual Wonkathon on rules for digital technology in schools.
points: Pondiscio frames the Hannah-Jones story as a lesson that reform must pursue both accountability for results and the competence to deliver them.
Freitag takes the position that AI bans are the wrong lever and that regulators should wait to observe real classroom impact.
Churchill commends Ohio for adopting automatic enrollment in advanced math and notes it pushes districts to create accelerated options where none exist.
A dual-enrollment review asks whether students still gain something when they fail the college courses they enrolled in.
A Washington State study finds no-zero grading policies rose by 110 percent over ten years across 295 districts.
quotes: Nikole Hannah-Jones’s experience with her daughter’s failing elementary school offers an important lesson: Good schools require both responsibility and competence.

The next task for education reform is therefore not merely helping parents identify good schools. It is understanding what makes schools good—and figuring out how to make effective practice routine rather than exceptional.
Her conclusion is that AI is both a huge opportunity for learning and a big risk—a tool to do great or horrible things.
She also believes that speculations about what will be good or bad are often wrong, so we should wait and observe real-world impacts before regulating the technology.

Following in the footsteps of North Carolina and Texas, Ohio is now among the states that have adopted automatic-enrollment math policies. The change is a good one, as it promises to help ensure that all high achievers are challenged to reach their potential.

Efforts to increase access to dual-enrollment programs have led to more high schoolers than ever taking college courses. This has many upsides, but it also increases the likelihood that more unprepared students will enroll in them and fail.

A new study maps the policy landscape of no-zero grading. It examines 295 traditional school districts in Washington State, covering 2015–16 through 2024–25, and finds, among other things, that no-zero grading policies increased by 110 percent over those ten years.
